blocks.text: Dear Ms. Ward:

It was a pleasure to spend the last several weeks talking through the pricing questions that {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} is weighing, and I am writing now to set down, in terms I hope read as plainly as those conversations did, the basis on which our firm would carry the work forward, so that once you have read this letter and, if it reflects our understanding, signed it below, there is a single document to which either of us can return should a question ever arise about what we agreed. I have tried throughout to describe what we will do, and what we will charge for doing it, in language that claims only as much as I am confident the firm can stand behind, and if any passage here strikes you as promising more than that, I would far rather you raised it with me before you signed than let it pass unremarked.
The Question We Have Been Asked to Take Up

As I understand the assignment, {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} has reached the point where the way it sets and manages its prices deserves a considered look from outside, and you have asked us to give the pricing across the principal lines of the business a disciplined examination and to come back to you with a strategy you can act on. Our work will run from an orderly reading of how prices are arrived at today, through a comparison against what the market and the nearest competitors will bear, to a set of recommendations on where price can be held, where it can prudently be moved, and how the discipline for setting it might be put on a firmer footing than it now rests on. What the engagement does not extend to is the running of your commercial operation, which remains entirely yours to direct, nor to legal, tax, or accounting advice, on which you should continue to rely on the advisers who ordinarily provide it; where our analysis touches those matters, what we offer is a reasoned business view and not a professional opinion in their place.
The Manner in Which We Would Work

Our way of working is deliberate, and I hope you will find it plain in its manner rather than clever in it. We begin by listening, to you and to the people who already carry a working view of how your prices are built, and only then do we set down the small number of judgments the pricing truly turns on and build the analysis outward from those, so that every figure we eventually place in front of you can be traced back to where it came from. Where the evidence will support a firm recommendation we will give you one, and where it will support only a range or a caution we will tell you that instead, because a recommendation that outruns what we actually know is of no use to you and no credit to us.
The People Who Would Carry It

I will keep my own hand on the engagement and will read anything of consequence before it leaves the firm under our name, but the daily work would sit with three of our people whom I would ask you to come to know. Brenda Rodriguez, a Senior Consultant, would carry the analytical core of the assignment and own the pricing model on which the recommendations rest; Deborah Gordon, an Associate, would take the benchmarking and the comparison against the market, work that lives in the spreadsheets as much as in the memos; and Mary Parker, a Research Associate, would assemble the company and market background that grounds the whole, and would keep the sources on file so that no figure we cite is ever left without a home. You are welcome to reach me at any time, though for most day-to-day matters one of the three named here will be the quicker route to an answer.
Fee and Payment

Our fee for the engagement as I have described it is {{fact:f:E-2009-004.fee}}, which covers the time of the people named above through the close of the work. We will render invoices against that amount as the work proceeds, and each will be payable within thirty days of your receipt of it. The fee covers our people and their time and not the incidental costs of the assignment, such as travel or the reproduction of materials, which we will incur only with your agreement and pass through to you at what they cost us; and should the shape of the work change materially from what this letter contemplates, I will raise the question of the fee with you and we will settle it together before any further work is done, so that nothing ever reaches you on an invoice as a surprise.
Term

The engagement would begin on {{fact:f:E-2009-004.start}} and we expect it to run for something on the order of seven months, though I would ask you to treat that as an honest estimate of the work rather than a promise about the calendar, since we will regard the assignment as complete when it is genuinely done and not merely when a given number of months has passed. Either of us may bring the engagement to an end on thirty days' written notice to the other, and if you choose to do so you will owe us for the work properly performed to that point and for any costs already committed on your behalf, and for nothing beyond that.
Confidentiality

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} in the course of this work we will hold in confidence and use only for the purposes of the engagement. That obligation binds every member of the team, it survives the end of our work together, and it covers the fact of our involvement as fully as it covers its substance. We would ask the same of you in respect of the methods and the written materials we share with you, which represent the firm's own way of working and are meant for your use and not for wider circulation.
Limitation of Liability

We will perform the work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect of a firm engaged for it, and we stand behind what we do. We do not, however, control the commercial decisions that {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} will ultimately take on the strength of our advice, nor the conditions of the markets in which you price and sell, and so, save to the extent the law does not permit such a limit, our liability to you arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees paid under it.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our firm is established, and any dispute arising under it will be determined by the courts of that state. Should any single provision of this letter be held unenforceable, the remainder of it will continue in force, unaffected.

If this letter sets out the understanding we reached, I would be grateful if you would sign one copy where indicated below and return it to me, keeping the other for your own file; once your signed copy is in my hands, Mary Parker will write to you to fix the first meetings and the initial requests for information, so that we can begin without delay.

To: Deborah Gordon and Brenda Rodriguez
From: Mary Parker
Re: Getting the pricing engagement for {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} under way

Now that the engagement for {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} has opened, on {{fact:f:E-2009-004.start}}, I want to put down in one place how we have agreed to divide the early work, so that the three of us start in step and none of us duplicates what another is already holding. Our aim in these first weeks is narrow and practical: to understand how the client sets and manages its prices today, and to gather the market and competitor context we will need, before any of us forms a view about what should change. Nothing in this phase produces a recommendation; it produces a clean, shared picture of the present state that the later analysis can stand on.
The work divides into five streams. I have put them in the order we expect to lean on them, since the present-state reading has to be at least under way before the benchmark means much:

items: 1. Present-state pricing. Brenda Rodriguez will document how prices are arrived at today across the main lines of the business, drawing on the client's own pricing files and a short round of interviews, and will note where the logic is consistent and where it is not. This is the stream the others depend on, so it goes first.

2. Market and competitor benchmark. Deborah Gordon will build the comparison against what the market and the nearest competitors are charging, keeping the workbook structured so a single figure can always be traced back to its source. Deborah will hold off on any read of the gaps until the present-state numbers are firm enough to compare against.

3. Company and market background. Mary Parker will assemble the profile of the client's markets and the peers worth watching, with the sources filed as they come in, to frame where price has room to move and where it does not.
4. Data requests to the client. All of us will feed a single list of the documents and contacts we each need, which I will consolidate so that the client sees one request from us and not three.
5. Working file. I will open the shared engagement file this week and keep it current, so that every figure and source we rely on has one home and none of us is working from a private copy.

blocks.text: Our sponsor on the client side is Barbara Ward, the Director of Operations, and I will route our requests for data and access through her so that the client hears one voice from us rather than several. She has asked that anything we need in the first month reach her in a single consolidated note, which is the reason for the fourth stream above; she has also offered to make the pricing owners on her side available for the interviews Brenda will want, once we tell her which lines we are starting with.

On cadence, I propose a short standing check-in among the three of us once a week, kept to fifteen minutes and to the question of what is blocked, and a separate note to Barbara Ward only when we have something to ask for or to report. I would rather we not bury her under traffic in the first weeks, when the useful thing we can send her is a clean request and not a running commentary.

The one thing I need from each of you this week is your list of the documents and contacts your stream will require, sent to me by Friday, so that I can fold it into one request and get it to Barbara Ward before the weekend; I will keep the shared engagement file current as material arrives and post a short index of what we have and what is still outstanding, so that no one has to ask me twice for the same status.
Barbara,

Thank you for getting us set up so quickly. The pricing work for {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} is moving on schedule, and I wanted to line up the last of the data we need before we lose any time waiting on it. On our side the streams are all under way: Deborah Gordon has the market and competitor benchmark started, Brenda Rodriguez is into the present-state pricing files, and I am filling in the company and market background.

The gap now is on the pricing detail itself. Three of the schedules we asked for, the ones behind the two largest product lines, have not yet reached us, and Brenda cannot close out the present-state picture without them. If someone on your team can send those over by the middle of next week, we will stay comfortably on track.

I would also like to hold a short working call to walk you through what the benchmark is showing before we go any wider with it. For that call I have you, Barbara Ward, with Mary Parker and Deborah Gordon from our side; Brenda Rodriguez will join if the schedule allows. Could you let me know a half hour that suits you next week, and I will send the three outstanding schedules straight to Deborah the moment they arrive.
Thanks
Barbara,

Thank you, the two schedules came through this morning and Deborah Gordon already has them; that leaves just the third, for the smaller of the two product lines, still to come whenever your team can lay hands on it. With what we now have, Brenda Rodriguez can close out most of the present-state pricing picture for {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}} this week, and I will have the market background filled in alongside it.

For the working call, the half hour you offered on Thursday works well for us. I will send round a short agenda beforehand so no one is reading the benchmark cold, and I will keep it to what the numbers actually support rather than getting ahead of the analysis. If it helps, I am happy to send the benchmark workbook a day early so you can look at the product-line gaps before we talk them through.

One ask before then: it would help to have you, Barbara Ward, confirm who on your side owns the pricing for that third product line, so Brenda Rodriguez can put a question or two to them directly. If you can send me that name, I will fold it into the agenda and copy Deborah Gordon and Mary Parker so we are all working from the same list.
Thanks
Pricing Strategy: {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}}

An interim briefing on the pricing engagement, prepared for Barbara Ward and the leadership team by the Calderwood engagement team. This is a read-out of where the work sits and what we are asking of you, not a set of conclusions; those come later, and only once the numbers behind them are settled with your team.
Where the Engagement Stands

items: The engagement opened on {{fact:f:E-2009-004.start}} and is in its early weeks.
We are still gathering and reconciling the present-state picture, so nothing here is a recommendation yet.
Where a figure is still moving, we have said so rather than round it off to look finished.
Today's purpose is to share what the work has surfaced so far and to agree the questions worth pursuing next.

blocks.text: Your Engagement Team

items: Brenda Rodriguez, Senior Consultant, owns the present-state pricing and the pricing model the recommendations will rest on.
Deborah Gordon, Associate, leads the market and competitor benchmark and the workbook behind it.
Mary Parker, Research Associate, assembles the company and market background and keeps every source on file.

blocks.text: What the Work Has Shown So Far

items: Prices are set consistently in the largest line, but the logic varies line to line elsewhere, which is where the early attention belongs.
Because that logic varies, the same product can carry different margins depending on who quoted it.
The benchmark points to room to move on a handful of mid-volume products where the firm is priced below the nearest competitors.
A small number of pricing schedules are still being reconciled with your team before we treat the present-state picture as settled.

blocks.text: The Questions Ahead

items: Where price can be held, where it can prudently be moved, and by how much the evidence will actually support.
How much of the apparent room to move is durable, as against a competitor's short-term promotion we should not chase.
How to put the discipline for setting price on a firmer footing than it now rests on.
Which changes the organization can absorb first without unsettling what is already working.

blocks.text: Next Steps

items: Close out the remaining pricing schedules with your team this week.
Hold the working session to review the benchmark in full.
Separate the durable price gaps from the promotion-driven ones before anything is proposed.
Agree the two or three questions the strategy turns on, so the next phase begins with a clear mandate.

blocks.text: Working Session Minutes: Pricing Strategy for {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}}

The session settled the main question we came in with: the benchmark holds up, and there is real room to move price on a defined set of products, but not the blanket increase some had expected. Two things still stand in the way of sizing that move, one schedule the client owes us and a clear list of the customer commitments that cannot be reset quickly, and both have owners and dates below. The rest of these minutes record how the group got there and who carries what next.
Present

items: Brenda Rodriguez, Senior Consultant, Calderwood Partners (chair)
Deborah Gordon, Associate, Calderwood Partners
Mary Parker, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
Barbara Ward, Director of Operations, {{fact:f:E-2009-004.client}}

blocks.text: Discussion

Deborah Gordon walked the group through the benchmark. Against the nearest competitors, the firm is priced at or above the market on its largest line and below it on a cluster of mid-volume products. Deborah was careful to separate the products where the gap is real and durable from those where it reflects a competitor's short-term promotion, and the group agreed that only the first group is worth acting on now.

Brenda Rodriguez reported that the present-state pricing picture is now closed for every line but the smallest, which is still waiting on one schedule from the client. The main finding is that price is set consistently in the largest line and by looser rules elsewhere, so the same product can carry different margins depending on who quoted it. Barbara Ward confirmed that pattern from her own side and noted that some of the softer pricing is tied to older customer commitments that cannot be reset quickly. The group agreed the recommendation has to distinguish what can change on the next quote from what has to wait for those commitments to run their course.

Mary Parker presented the market and competitor background that frames the benchmark, and flagged two competitors whose pricing has moved in the last quarter and is worth watching before any change goes out. She kept the read narrow, on the products where the movement is recent enough to matter, and put the rest aside as noise for now. Deborah Gordon agreed to fold that watch into the benchmark workbook so the two views do not drift apart.

The group left one question open on purpose: whether to test a price change on a single product line first or move on the whole eligible set at once. Barbara Ward argued for a single line, on the ground that it is easier to walk back if a customer pushes; Brenda Rodriguez noted that a one-line test also gives us a clean before-and-after to learn from. No one pressed for the full set today. The call itself is the leadership's to make, and it will go to them framed as a choice rather than as our conclusion.
Actions

rows: Sort the benchmark products into a durable-gap group and a promotion-driven group, and drop the second
Close the present-state picture on the smallest line once the last schedule arrives
Send the client the last outstanding pricing schedule and confirm which commitments are fixed
Refresh the two moving competitors before any change is drafted

blocks.text: The one thing that has to happen before we meet again is action 3: without the last schedule and a clear read on the fixed commitments, we cannot size the change. Once Barbara Ward's team sends those over, Brenda Rodriguez will set the next session to review a first draft of the recommendation.
